title: GPU memory moat and adaptive cushion for continuous batching
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: introduce a lightweight, tenant-aware 'memory moat' (adaptive headroom) that sits between weight residency, KV cache allocation, and transient activations to reduce OOMs and noisy preemptions during continuous batching. The design must be compatible with Dedicated and Private deployments and expose controls in the console for aggressive vs conservative cushion profiles.

Scope: algorithm and runtime hook for computing GPU-level and tenant-level moat, integration with existing KV cache accounting and eviction, metrics and telemetry for moat utilization, and a canary rollout with telemetry-driven throttle for aggressive shrink.

Key ideas: compute moat as a probabilistic cushion composed of three signals: a moving-percentile (e.g., 95th) of recent activation peaks, a forecasted short-horizon KV growth (token-based scan), and a weight-safety floor based on pinned model residency. Moat size is smoothed by exponential backoff to avoid oscillation; when pressure exceeds moat the runtime initiates a graded soft-preempt sequence (evict cold KV shards -> compress active KV -> spill prefetch candidates to CPU) before hard OOM.

Trade-offs considered: larger moats reduce tail OOMs but increase overall reserved GPU capacity (cost). Fast shrink policies improve utilization but risk transient OOMs for bursty tenants. We chose an asymmetric policy: rapid expansion on pressure spikes, conservative shrink only after sustained low pressure (configurable decay window).
comments: 2026-03-02 — Kickoff meeting: aligned on moat concept, owners, and compatibility constraints with Dedicated/Private. Action: Marco to prototype estimator; Aisha to draft console UX controls.

2026-03-05 — Prototype results: moving-95th activation percentile + KV delta gave stable cushion for 70% of test tenants; worst-case tenant still experienced OOM under synthetic 5x burst. Added soft-preempt sequence to prototype which avoided OOMs in subsequent runs.

2026-03-08 — Design review: PM (Lena Cho) requested explicit per-tenant 'burst window' knob and a global cost-budget cap. Security reviewed no new surface for KMS. Decision: surface two profiles (conservative, aggressive) and advanced controls via API only initially.
2026-03-10 — Implementation: merged kv-accounting shim and exposed moat delta metric (redwood.moat_utilization). Started unit tests for shrink/expand behavior (edge windows).

2026-03-12 — Testing: canary on staging fleet (10% capacity) with production-like token distribution. Observed moat kept OOMs near-zero and reduced KV eviction churn by 38% vs baseline. Performance note: median token latency unchanged, P99 latency increased 3% under extreme synthetic bursts — investigating whether preempt sequence ordering can be optimized.
acceptance_criteria: Canary run (2 weeks) shows zero hard OOMs for tenants in canary under production workload
Moat utilization metric is emitted and available in Console per-tenant and aggregated GPU-level
KV eviction churn reduced by >=25% compared to baseline in canary
Expose profile toggle (conservative/aggressive) in Console feature flag for early access
Runtime falls back to existing eviction path on regression or misconfiguration without service disruption
rollout_plan: Phase 1: Staging canary (10% capacity) for 2 weeks; collect moat_utilization, eviction_churn, tail-latency. Phase 2: Gradual ramp to 30% with per-region flags if metrics stable. Phase 3: Enable tenant opt-in via Console API, monitor cost delta. Phase 4: Full ramp with automated shrink/expand enabled when cost-sla checks pass. Rollback: disable adaptive moat and revert to baseline eviction policy via runtime flag.
